2bc04e533d21fd4c: OpenAI has detailed the extent of the dirty deeds its agents indulged in Down Under in a Tuesday blog post titled How we will do better for Australia, which addresses last week’s news that one of its models improperly accessed a website that stores data related to national health scheme Medicare. “Our models accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not authorised to,” the post opens. “We also should have handled our response better. We are sorry and working to do better in the future.” The post offers some new detail on the Medicare incident, saying that it involved “an experimental, internal-only OpenAI model that was not intended for public release and without the full set of safeguards used in our publicly available products.” OpenAI gave the model the job of researching government spending per person on medicines for skin conditions in one Australian state. “The model had difficulty obtaining that information, and it took actions that we had not authorised it to take,” OpenAI admitted. “In the course of looking for this information at Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics Reporting Service, it discovered a way to gain non-public access to the service. It then used this access to review technical system information and source code related to the service – all still with the objective of trying to find the information it was originally looking for.” The Register last week asked OpenAI if the company conducted the tests itself or used a partner. The company did not respond to our request. In another incident disclosed in the new post, the company’s bots visited the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare and tried, unsuccessfully, to bypass access controls. The agents were still able to retrieve statistics using third-party browsing and download services, including from the institute’s website. “The downloaded material appears to have been publicly available. There was no system compromise. Individual medical records were not accessed,” OpenAI wrote. The company didn’t report the incident because it “did not meet our disclosure thresholds because the way it was accessed seemed consistent with public access.” OpenAI changed its mind and notified the Institute on 24 September – the day Australia’s prime minister announced the Medicare incident. Another concerning incident took place at the State of Victoria’s Agency for Health Information, which OpenAI agents visited after they “discovered an exposed access key.” The agent used that key to “retrieve reporting configuration and aggregate survey statistics.” OpenAI has given itself a pass on this one, writing “The extent to which this information should have been accessible is unclear, and depends on VAHI’s access policies. Individual medical records or identifiable survey responses were not accessed.” A fourth incident revealed in the post saw OpenAI agents visit the State of New South Wales’ Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and make API and website metadata requests using a public-facing research tool. OpenAI has promised it will “commit the resources needed to help affected agencies understand what happened and assess the impact” – whatever that means. It’s also donating credits for the Daybreak cyber-defense service and promised to “establish a taskforce with independent Australian expertise to develop practical policy recommendations for managing risks from increasingly capable AI agents.” That taskforce “will focus on improving notification processes, strengthening coordination between AI developers and government, and identifying measures to better protect government systems.” OpenAI wants the taskforce to deliver recommendations by the end of 2026. The post is very much of the “We’re sorry and we promise to do better in future” genre, pioneered by Meta and popular with entities that leak data or experience outages. The Register expects more of the same sentiments next week, when OpenAI’s Chief Strategy Officer, Jason Kwon, appears before the Australian Senate’s Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence. “He will answer questions about what we know, how we responded, what steps we have taken, and how we will do better going forward,” OpenAI says. ®

a1056c0e0ac5f437: Saya mulakan penulisan ini dengan mengimbau kembali sedutan ucapan penggulungan Sanusi Nor selaku pengarah pilihan raya PAS pada muktamar PAS pada 16 Sept 2025.

Kata Sanusi, pada PRU15, parti rakan dalam Perikatan Nasional (PN) bergantung pada peralatan yang terpaksa dibayar oleh PAS: "Semua peralatan kita bayar, mereka datang bertanding sahaja, lepas tu nak jadi ketua tapi duit tak ada dan jentera tak ada."
Dan kata beliau lagi, "Jangan sampai kita ungkit semua”. Sebenarnya apa yang diucapkan itu sudah pun boleh dianggap 'mengungkit'.

Sindiran Sanusi umum tahu ditujukan kepada Muhyiddin Yassin dan partinya Bersatu yang ketika itu duduk bersama PAS dalam PN. Tidak lama kemudian, hubungan antara dua parti itu mulai renggang. The rest is history.

Imbau pula ucapan Sanusi pada muktamar PAS 2026 awal bulan ini. “PAS ni sudah jadi parti gajah. Tiba tiba lalu kucing bawa anak dua tiga ekor ... jadi takut." Rasanya ramai sudah tonton video ucapan itu.
Jika pernah ikuti, tentu anda ingat apa lagi kata beliau: "Jangan ikut kucing tu, dia pun baru nak hidup ja Dia baru tubuh parti dua hari lepas, dok ajar kita lepas tu kita turut dia, tak betul tu."

Siapa yang Sanusi maksudkan? Mana parti yang baru ditubuhkan? Mungkinkah Wawasan? Wallahua'lam tetapi memang Wawasan baru ditubuhkan akibat masalah dalaman Bersatu. Ia parti serpihan Bersatu. Dan Wawasan baru diterima sebagai komponen PN.

Perhatikan beberapa sedutan ucapan Sanusi lagi: “Orang yang ada masalah pun, mai kat kita. Mereka nak cari ubat, suruh kita hembus, kita tolonglah hembus .Dah jadi sihat elok, jangan nak duduk atas kepala kita pulak."
“Pastu dah tak ada orang, ambil orang kita, lepas tu kita pi seronok. Orang kita pi kat dia, kita seronok. Lepas tu, parti dia besar, parti kita kecil. Dia jadi calon, kita jadi jentera.
“Orang mai menumpang kita, kita pula rasa kerdil. Bilik tidur kita, bagi kat dia, kita tidur ruang tamu ... banyak cantik!”

Adakah apa yang Sanusi huraikan itu sudah berlaku? Adakah parti yang baru 'berusia' dua hari dan punya masalah datang minta pertolongan PAS, tetapi sekarang sudah besar kepala, lantas buat tuntutan? Dah nak duduk atas kepala PAS?
Sanusi pemimpin kanan parti. Tentu beliau tahu apa yang ramai termasuk ahli PAS biasa tidak tahu.
Atau mungkin beliau 'sekadar' mengingatkan PAS supaya berhati-hati agar apa yang beliau kata tadi tidak terjadi?
Pun begitu, mesejnya jelas, yakni PAS jangan rasa diri kerdil.

Ini kerap beliau ulangi. Masalah orang PAS, rasa kerdil, padahal PAS sudah parti besar berusia 75 tahun, katanya. Namun bagi saya yang melihat PAS dari luar dan jauh, parti itu tidak pernah tunjuk tanda rasa diri kerdil. At least not in the open.
Malah ramai pemimpinnya bila bercakap kedengaran 'condifent' sehingga tahap overconfident dan appear arrogant. Bagaimanapun, Sanusi pada ucapannya menyentuh juga aspek 'deal'.
Maksudkan apabila pemimpin atau sesiapa yang mewakili PAS pergi berunding dengan pihak dalam dan luar PN, elemen 'kerdil' timbul, yang boleh atau sudah bawa sesal di belakang hari.
“Jangan lepas dok rugi, bagi semua kat orang, lepas tu menyesal mai dok meratap di sini."
Ini jelas merujuk rundingan pengagihan kerusi untuk ditandingi pada PRU atau PRN. Adakah rundingan atau meminjam istilah Sanusi, 'deal', membabitkan Wawasan?

Mungkin ya, tetapi runding dengan Wawasan tentang kerusi untuk dipertandingkan bukan masalah besar untuk PAS. Meskipun Presiden PAS Hadi Awang ada soft spot terhadap Hamzah Zainudin, iaitu presiden Wawasan, saya percaya PAS will not be cowed. Ibarat parti gajah dengan parti kucing. Sekali lagi meminjam istilah yang digunakan Sanusi.
Maka menurut saya, selain rundingan dalam PN, apa yang diperkatakan Sanusi pada ucapannya merujuk lebih kepada seat negotiation dengan parti besar, umpamanya Umno.
Mesej Sanusi adalah pemimpin dan juru runding PAS mesti berani mempertahankan pendirian. “Kerusi kita jangan diserahkan."

Menghayati apa yang dikatakan Sanusi, mesejnya, menurut saya, ditujukan kepada kepimpinan PAS, iaitu sama ada runding dengan parti luar PN (boleh dibaca Umno), apa lagi dengan komponen (Wawasan, Pejuang, Gerakan, MIPP), PAS mesti jadi tuan.
Meskipun mesej disampaikan menerusi ucapan 5 Sept lalu, saya kira pendirian Sanusi tidak berubah.

7a387d07c6bfd33b: From Moaz Nair
In Peninsular Malaysia, the road to Putrajaya remains dogmatically unchanged: whoever commands the Malay geopolitical heartland commands the federal government.
Demographic projections across the peninsula’s 165 parliamentary seats clearly draw the battle lines for GE16.

The numbers do not lie. A crushing 86 seats constitute hardcore Malay strongholds (with a demographic composition of 65% and above), 32 seats stand as moderate Malay-majority areas (51% to 64%), while the remaining 47 are mixed or non-Malay-majority constituencies.
Strip away the noise, and the reality is stark: these 86 absolute-majority seats hold the ultimate monopoly on power.
For decades, this golden threshold was the exclusive battleground of a duopoly between Umno and PAS. Yet GE16 is primed to violently rip apart this traditional bipolar landscape.

The desperate survival struggles of a cornered Bersatu, combined with the fracturing foundations of the Pakatan Harapan-Barisan Nasional ruling coalition, are dragging this traditional heartland into unprecedented political anarchy.
To grasp why consensus is now an absolute impossibility, one must look at the structural devastation of GE15.

The ferocious momentum of the Green Wave — weaponised by the aggressive machinery of PAS — engineered a total sweep of 14 seats in Kelantan and eight in Terengganu, before utterly obliterating rivals in Perlis and Kedah.
This surge propelled Perikatan Nasional (PN) to a commanding 73 seats, while the Umno-led BN suffered a humiliating collapse, barely salvaging 30 seats.
Today, PAS stands at the absolute peak of geopolitical arrogance, wielding total dominance over the “SG4” state governments.
In the ruthless arena of realpolitik, it is pure delusion to expect PAS to voluntarily surrender its conquered territories to an Umno that is still stumbling through a painful rehabilitation phase.
Concurrently, the opposition bloc faces a crippling internal crisis as Bersatu completely loses its teeth.
The party that once proudly postured as the ultimate kingmaker — bridging the gap between conservative and urban Malay voters — is now rotting from internal fragmentation.
The entry of new factions like Parti Wawasan Negara further erodes Bersatu’s fragile grip on traditional PN seats.
Sensing this profound weakness, PAS has shown zero hesitation in sidelining Bersatu to negotiate directly with Umno.
In Pahang, PAS has already mobilised its machinery into Bersatu territory. For PAS, Bersatu is no longer an equal partner; it is a bleeding strategic liability.

This calculated predatory move fundamentally rewrites the political math: if PAS swallows Bersatu to split the Malay heartland with Umno, a brutal zero-sum war will erupt for the ultimate title of sole custodian of the Malay-Muslim narrative.
Across the aisle, the unity government is staring down an existential nightmare.
The marriage between Anwar Ibrahim’s PH and Ahmad Zahid Hamidi’s BN was forged as a desperate post-GE15 lifeline, completely devoid of ideological synergy.
As grassroots fury within Umno hits critical mass, the shelf life of this unnatural alliance is rapidly expiring.

Umno’s core loyalists will never accept sharing a bed with PH, let alone the DAP. To avert total extinction in GE16, Umno is desperate to prove to the Malay electorate that its dignity was not traded away for raw power.
Consequently, Umno has begun playing a dangerous double game, leaving the back door wide open for backroom talks with PAS to explore an alternative Malay-Muslim alliance.
However, this two-faced posturing is a ticking time bomb.
It is logistically and rhetorically impossible for Umno to campaign for PH in urban strongholds while simultaneously trying to wrestle rural heartlands from PAS.
The moment seat negotiations commence, these irreconcilable agendas will completely paralyse BN’s campaign machinery.

In the Westminster system, numbers are absolute. Umno is driven by a vengeful obsession to reclaim its historical dominance, while PAS, now the undisputed titan at the federal level, has absolutely no reason to yield without demanding the lion’s share of power.
To expect a peaceful resolution or a clean consensus on seat distribution for GE16 is an act of sheer political naivety.
The current reality blares a deafening warning: when the election war horns sound, the battle for the Malay political heartland will devolve into a vicious, multi-cornered bloodbath.
Any party that fails to ruthlessly recalibrate its survival strategy will face swift political execution by the voters at the ballot box.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

Tetapi, jangan kita pening sangat dengan siapa Umno mahu 'kahwin'. Soalan yang lebih penting ialah: Umno hari ini cukup kuatkah untuk memilih, atau sebenarnya sedang mencari sesiapa yang boleh membantunya bertahan?
Desakan supaya Umno mendekati PAS memang semakin kuat dan suara itu kedengaran jelas dalam parti. Tetapi jerit kuat tidak semestinya bermakna kedudukan politik juga kuat.
Bacaan saya mudah. Umno perlukan bantuan.

Dalam pertandingan tiga penjuru, matematiknya tidak menyebelahi Umno semudah yang cuba digambarkan sesetengah pemimpinnya. Sebab itu PAS menjadi menarik. Bukan kerana tiba-tiba kedua-duanya menemui formula hebat untuk Malaysia, tetapi kerana angka undi nampak lebih sedap apabila dicampurkan.
PAS tambah Umno, atas kertas memang nampak 'ong'.
Masalahnya, kalau Umno memerlukan PAS lebih daripada PAS memerlukan Umno, siapa sebenarnya akan menentukan syarat?
Itu perkara yang penyokong kerjasama ini perlu fikir.
PAS sudah mempunyai tapak kukuh di Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah dan Perlis. Kalau empat negeri itu dianggap kawasan PAS, apa yang tinggal untuk Umno?
Johor, Melaka dan Negeri Sembilan?
Bagaimana pula Selangor, Perak dan Pahang? Kalau perlu dibahagi juga, semakin kecil ruang Umno untuk mendakwa dirinya pemain utama dalam perkongsian itu.
Politik bukan sekadar campur undi dan kira siapa dapat lebih banyak kerusi. Selepas menang, ada satu lagi soalan: siapa bos?
Umno mungkin masuk dengan sejarah panjang sebagai parti yang pernah menguasai kerajaan persekutuan. PAS pula akan masuk dengan kekuatan akar umbi dan negeri yang kini menjadi kubunya.
Jadi jangan anggap 'kahwin' itu automatik menjadikan kedua-duanya pasangan sama taraf.
Kalau satu pihak lebih kuat, satu pihak lagi akhirnya kena ikut.
Di situlah masalah Umno. Parti itu mahu dilihat masih besar, tetapi pada masa sama kelihatan memerlukan rakan untuk mengelakkan dirinya daripada tersepit dalam pertandingan pelbagai penjuru.
Mahu duduk semeja dengan PAS boleh. Tetapi kalau datang ke meja dengan kerusi sendiri pun tidak cukup kukuh, jangan terkejut kalau orang lain menentukan menu.
Kemudian ada pula soal dasar dan hala tuju.

PAS mempunyai pendirian sendiri mengenai perlembagaan, pentadbiran dan pelbagai isu negara. Umno pula selama ini mahu membawa imej parti Melayu yang lebih luas dan mempunyai sejarah bekerja dengan pelbagai parti komponen.
Apabila kedua-duanya bersama, siapa akan mengikut siapa?
Itu bukan soalan kecil. Ia akan menentukan bukan sahaja pembahagian kerusi tetapi juga wajah kerajaan yang mahu dibentuk.
Kemudian kita sampai kepada soalan paling sedap: kalau gabungan itu berkuasa, siapa jadi perdana menteri?
Umno mahu jawatan itu? PAS tentu ada perkiraannya sendiri.
Kalau Umno masuk ke dalam kerjasama dalam keadaan lebih lemah, atas alasan apa PAS perlu menyerahkan kedudukan paling atas kepadanya?
Inilah perkara yang saya rasa lebih penting daripada segala jeritan tentang mahu bersama siapa dan mahu meninggalkan siapa.
Umno perlu bertanya kepada dirinya sendiri: apa sebenarnya yang dibawa ke meja rundingan?
Kerusi? Undi? Negeri? Kepimpinan? Atau sekadar nama besar daripada zaman lalu?
Isu Negeri Sembilan juga menunjukkan betapa rumitnya kedudukan parti itu apabila percaturan di peringkat negeri boleh membawa kesan jauh lebih besar kepada imej dan hubungan politiknya.
Semakin banyak percaturan dibuat, semakin banyak pula Umno perlu menjelaskan kepada rakyat apa sebenarnya pendiriannya.
Sebab itu bagi saya, sebelum bercakap besar tentang PAS atau PH, ukuran paling mudah ialah kekuatan Umno sendiri.
Kalau sebuah parti benar-benar kuat, ia tidak perlu terlalu risau siapa mahu bersamanya. Orang lain yang akan datang mengetuk pintu.

Kalau setiap kali pilihan raya perlu mencari formula siapa punya undi boleh ditumpang, siapa punya kubu boleh dikongsi dan siapa boleh membantu elak kekalahan tiga penjuru, itu bukan tanda kuasa tawar yang hebat.
Itu tanda ada masalah. Umno boleh memilih siapa sahaja sebagai rakan politik. Itu urusan mereka.
Tetapi 'kahwin' dengan PAS tidak secara ajaib menjadikan Umno lebih kuat. Keluar daripada kerajaan perpaduan juga tidak dengan sendirinya mengembalikan zaman kegemilangannya.
Akhirnya politik sangat mudah. Kalau kuat, tunjuk kuat.
Kalau masih perlukan orang lain untuk nampak kuat, jangan marah apabila orang bertanya siapa sebenarnya yang memimpin siapa.

5d573d80c639ec50: Is AI a bubble? It all depends, we are told, on whether massive investments in the technology will massively boost productivity. Optimists are convinced that future productivity gains will be colossal, even if a market correction is necessary to draw some hot air out of the current boom.
Pessimists, from Goldman Sachs’ Jim Covello to MIT’s Daron Acemoglu, have their doubts. But optimists and pessimists alike are in the grip of what I call the AI productivity delusion.

What both sides miss is that AI will devastate capitalism even if it boosts productivity beyond our imaginations—and regardless of whether it delivers the promised economy-wide automation of everyday corporate workflows.
The reason why we tend to miss this point is that we look at today’s world through the lens of another world that cloud capital, especially now that it is AI-enhanced, has rendered obsolete.

Until recently, it was a foregone conclusion that every technological revolution represents a moment of creative destruction. Whole sectors, professions, and skill sets were destroyed by innovations which ushered in new sectors, new professions, and new skill sets.

Automobiles ruined saddlers, farriers, and knackers but begat auto workers, road builders, mechanics, and service-station personnel. The transition from coal to oil condemned whole mining communities, not to mention trade unions, to oblivion. In net terms, however, more was created than was destroyed. Creative destruction became synonymous with economic growth.

Faced with the AI juggernaut, it is natural to focus on the technology’s net effects. Will it create more than it destroys? But the real question is, “More of what?” To avoid the AI productivity delusion, we must rethink how we define productivity.

If by productivity we mean tasks accomplished per unit of human labour, there is no doubt that AI will prove an immense success—in fact, it already has. But, if we continue to measure productivity in terms of monetary value produced per unit of labour, the chances are that AI will prove to be an unmitigated disaster.
Earlier technological revolutions, from the steam engine and the automobile to the personal computer and the smartphone, expanded the domain of capitalist markets.
Despite the wreckage of whole professions and communities they left in their wake, they resulted in simultaneously more material output and a higher aggregate monetary value of that output.
Will AI do likewise? Maybe in China, where AI is coupled with robotics, material production will rise and, at least in the short run, so will net revenues.

But in the West, AI agents are deployed in the service sector—from amazon.com to back offices, law firms, hospitals, and more. In those domains, AI-enhanced cloud capital could shrink markets in two distinct ways.

The first way, the one everyone worries about, is that AI will kill off entire professions: paralegals, coders, translators, accountants, even architects, mathematicians, and school teachers, while creating far fewer new jobs filled by the prompters, overseers, engineers, and operators of the new machinery. The second way is far less visible but perhaps even more worrying: the conversion of markets into cloud fiefs and of profits into rents.
As I argued long ago, Amazon may look like a market, with countless buyers and sellers within its digital walls, but it lacks the central feature of a market: decentralisation.

In fact, it is more centralised than the Soviet planned economy ever was, with an inscrutable algorithm deciding which consumer is matched to which vendor on the basis of a probabilistic model optimised to maximise the likelihood that Jeff Bezos, its owner, collects 40% of the maximum price every customer is willing to pay.
As AI becomes more deeply embedded in Bezos’s algorithm, interfaces like Alexa will communicate with us not as mere shopping assistants but as an all-knowing friend, companion, and even therapist.

Soon, capitalist vendors’ profits will end up in some tech lord’s account in the form of cloud rent, which he will most certainly invest in more AI-enhanced cloud capital that produces more power to extract more cloud rents.

So, as Apple’s Siri, Google’s Gemini, and an army of such agentic assistants develop the same capacities for their tech lords as Amazon has for Bezos, the capitalist market domain will continue to shrink.

While AI will have proven exceedingly productive in terms of economic activities performed per unit of human labour, the profit rates of capitalist enterprises will collapse, following society’s aggregate wages to the bottom.

At that point, none of the tools of the liberal state—no amount of quantitative easing, no politically feasible levels of universal basic income, no wealth tax that the tech lords will find hard to evade—will be able to prevent a systemic collapse.

The question of whether AI will generate massive productivity gains is easy to answer: Yes. AI is already proving capable of exponentially increasing the amount of work that is being done per human worker.
But as long as it is used to eliminate wage labour while syphoning off profits from actual markets into our tech lords’ cloud rents, the economic value produced per worker will tank.

Unless this distinction is made, the AI productivity delusion will persist. And as long as it does, we will be unable to hope for a post-capitalist future of abundance where we, along with our AI helpers, produce according to ability and distribute according to need.
Yanis Varoufakis, a former finance minister of Greece, is leader of the MeRA25 party, professor of economics at the University of Athens, and a senior research fellow at Fudan University.

54df7ce6cc3cd628: Sudah selalu saya dengar rungutan karyawan tentang senang-senang sahaja orang ‘bukan karyawan’ menghasilkan karya kreatif menggunakan kecerdasan buatan atau AI dan kemudian mengiktiraf diri sendiri sebagai pengkarya tulen. Baru-baru ini di media sosial saya melihat penggiat muzik bercakap pasal ini dengan nada bengang.

Saya berada dalam lingkungan pelukis, penulis dan perekabentuk grafik. Mereka pun telah lama merungut tentangnya. Ada yang memang anti-AI terus. Sama seperti hujah penggiat muzik, kata mereka karya yang dihasilkan AI tidak mempunyai jiwa.

Karyawan ini mengatakan orang yang menggunakan AI untuk menghasilkan kerja seni tidak layak dipanggil karyawan. Mereka cuma menekan butang, kemudian mesin membuat semuanya. Bila siap, mendabik dada mengaku dia sudah mencipta lagu, membuat lukisan dan sebagainya. Bagi sebahagian karyawan, kehadiran AI dianggap sebagai pengancam periuk nasi dan punca pendapatan. Luahan ini memang wajar diberi perhatian serius dan tidak boleh dipandang enteng. Justeru, mari kita bincangkan isu ini dengan memfokuskan kepada bidang muzik dan lagu sebab industri tersebut lebih mudah difahami masyarakat kerana hari-hari kita menyanyi dan mendengar lagu.

Kalau dahulu sebuah syarikat mahu membuat ‘jingle’ atau muzik latar iklan komersial mungkin mereka perlu mencari komposer, penyusun (arranger), pemuzik dan studio. Hari ini, dengan adanya AI seseorang boleh duduk bersendirian di rumah, menaip beberapa arahan dan…tup! Tak sampai dua minit, sebuah lagu sudah tersedia. Penjimatan kos telah banyak dilakukan kerana kita telah ‘melompat’ tradisi pembuatan yang telah lama kita amalkan. Mudah, kan?

Kecewa dengan perkembangan ini, kita menolak karya AI dengan mencemik menyatakan ‘AI tidak ada jiwa’. Ya, memanglah. Tetapi kalau nak ikutkan bab jiwa, alat muzik seperti gitar dan piano pun tak berjiwa malah angkatan pemuzik lama pun pernah menolak ‘synthesizer’ dan ‘drum machine’ yang juga dikatakan tidak mempunyai perasaan. Itu kita faham, semua instrumen dan ‘software’ memang tidak pernah bercinta dan tidak juga pernah kecewa.

Namun begitu, kelebihan teknologi AI pula ialah ia bukan alat pasif seperti gitar. Gitar tidak boleh main sendiri bila disuruh, tetapi AI bila kita beri arahan, "buatkan saya lagu sedih, tempo perlahan, mood kecewa ditinggal kekasih", sekejap saja ‘dia’ buat.
“Eleh, memanglah boleh! Tapi lagu AI tetap tak ada jiwa.” tempelak karyawan lagu. Tak ada jiwa lagi, alasannya!

Tahukah anda ada satu kajian yang diterbitkan dalam jurnal ‘Frontiers in Psychology’ pada Ogos lalu, eksperimen ‘blind listening’ terhadap 71 peserta yang memang terlatih dalam bidang asas muzik. Mereka telah diperdengarkan dengan muzik yang dibuat oleh manusia, juga muzik yang dibuat seratus-peratus oleh AI, serta muzik yang dibuat dengan kerjasama manusia-AI. Mereka tidak diberitahu tentang itu. Menariknya, peserta yang memang mempunyai pengetahuan asas tentang muzik ini juga tidak dapat mengenal pasti dengan konsisten mana satu manusia dan mana satu mesin.

Rupanya ini ada sangkut-paut dengan psikologi. Apabila diberitahu awal lagu tersebut hasil janaan AI, penilaian kita akan berubah. Maknanya label ‘ini hasil AI’ sendiri boleh mempengaruhi bagaimana kita mendengar muzik. Kalau diberitahu sebuah lagu ditulis oleh seorang lelaki yang baru kematian isteri, sebelum lagu bermula pun kita sudah bersedia untuk bersedih. Sebaliknya kalau diberitahu lagu yang sama itu dibuat oleh AI, automatik kita akan mencipta persepsi.
Bagaimanapun, hujah ini tidaklah membuktikan bahawa muzik janaan AI sama nilainya dengan karya tulen yang dihasilkan oleh manusia. Ini penting untuk kita semua faham.

Saya sendiri sebenarnya seronok bermain-main dengan AI untuk menghasilkan lagu. Bukan untuk bisnes, sekadar seronok-seronok untuk berasa syok kononnya telah menghasilkan sesuatu. Saya tulis lirik, tentukan genre muzik, karakter vokal, jenis-jenis instrumen dan durasinya. Hasil pun keluar. Tak sedap, saya suruh lagi berulang kali sehinggalah dapat hasil yang mirip dengan apa yang saya mahu. Sebuah lagu telah dihasilkan. Sudah tentulah saya bukan komposer. Di sinilah kita harus memperkenalkan beberapa istilah untuk membezakannya.

Komposer ialah manusia mutlak yang mencipta muzik asal seperti melodi, harmoni atau struktur. Jika komposer ini buat lagu menggunakan AI sebagai sebahagian alat produksinya, dia tetap komposer. Tetapi kalau AI memainkan peranan lebih besar dalam susunan dan mengembangkan idea asalnya, mungkin istilah ‘AI-assisted composer’ lebih telus.

Kemudian ada orang seperti saya yang tidak menggubah muzik tetapi memberi arahan kepada AI, memilih hasil, mengulang ‘prompt’ sehingga mendapat hasil. Saya tidak keberatan dipanggil ‘prompter muzik’. Ada keputusan kreatif yang saya buat tetapi tidak bolehlah saya mendakwa menggubah lagu sedangkan ia sebenarnya dihasilkan mesin. Orang-orang yang seperti saya ini juga haruslah sedar diri dan jangan perasan. Begitu jugalah gelaran dalam kerja kreatif bidang seni yang lain.

Istilah-istilah ini mungkin tidak sesuai lagi kerana teknologi terlalu cepat bergerak sampaikan istilah pun tak sempat dicipta. Yang lebih penting bagi saya ialah kredit perlu telus. Kalau Ahmad hanya menulis lirik dan memberi arahan kepada AI, janganlah pada kredit ditulis ‘lagu dan muzik: Ahmad’. Dengan penuh tanggungjawab tulislah misalnya ‘lirik: Ahmad, muzik: dijana dengan AI’ dan ‘arahan kreatif/kurasi: Ahmad’. Kalau Ahmad mencipta melodinya sendiri kemudian AI membantu gubahan, tulislah ‘Komposer: Ahmad’ dan ‘susunan/produksi: bantuan AI. Saya rasa itu lebih adil.

AI tidak wajar diberi hak moral seperti manusia. Yang kita perlukan ialah ketelusan tentang proses supaya hak manusia yang benar-benar menyumbang dapat dikenal pasti. Masyarakat juga perlu dididik tentang perbezaan tersebut. Kalau kita hanya menjerit ‘AI tiada jiwa’, memang perbincangan kita akan tersangkut dan tidak akan ke mana. Kita kena selesaikan.

Saya faham kebimbangan pemuzik kerana saya juga dalam bidang penghasilan karya. Saya melukis dan menulis. Saya tergugat juga dengan kehadiran AI. Pelanggan yang dahulu membayar kami untuk kerja-kerja mereka bentuk, grafik atau ilustrasi buku kini boleh menghasilkannya sendiri dalam masa seminit sahaja dengan hanya membayar harga ‘subscribe’ bulanan serendah RM20. Pelanggan yang memperuntukkan beberapa ribu ringgit untuk ‘jingle’ pun kini boleh mendapatkannya dengan lebih cepat dan murah. Ini kerana masyarakat pun ‘peduli apa’ karya tersebut dihasilkan oleh manusia tulen atau mesin. Asal sedap, mereka terima saja.

Sebab itu soal hak cipta, kredit, bagaimana AI digunakan dan bagaimana pencipta asal dilindungi perlu dibincangkan dengan serius. Ini kerana AI sudah ada. Nak tak nak, kita terpaksa berhadapan dengannya. Mungkin di situlah jalan tengahnya. Lindungi hak pencipta asal. Berikan kredit berdasarkan sumbangan. Bezakan komposer dengan orang yang sekadar memberi prompt.

Tetapi pada masa sama, karyawan juga harus melihat apa yang berlaku di sekeliling. Jangan hanya anti-AI dan mempersoalkan teknologi apabila kena pada kita sahaja. Hari ini kita memesan makanan melalui skrin atau telefon, membayar sendiri di kaunter layan diri dan melakukan urusan bank melalui mesin serta aplikasi. Robot pula sudah melakukan sebahagian kerja manusia di restoran, gudang dan kilang. Kita seronok kerana ia memudahkan urusan kita tapi kita tak peduli juga dengan manusia yang sudah kehilangan kerja di situ.

Kita tidak kisah pun dengan robot yang menghantar roti canai ke meja kita. Kita berasa lebih senang ‘order’ di skrin daripada kita menghadap muka manusia sehingga akhirnya manusia pun tersingkir. Paling tidak seronok dilihat ialah pengkarya muzik yang menentang penggunaan AI untuk menghasilkan lagu itu, pada masa sama pula menggunakan AI untuk membuat poster konsert. Macam mana tu? Mana pergi sindiran 'tak ada jiwa' tadi?

Dalam menghadapi cabaran teknologi, kita manusia yang ada jiwa inilah harus bersikap berani dan terbuka. Jika persaingan menjadi semakin sengit, kita tak boleh berterusan merengek dan merintih. Kita harus sambut cabaran, kuasai juga teknologi tersebut supaya kita tidak ketinggalan zaman.

ccbd0daf5a471290: On Sept 24, US president Donald Trump met Chinese president Xi Jinping in Washington. As leaders of the two most powerful countries, they preside over the world’s most consequential bilateral relationship. But if Trump assumes that this means China’s foreign policy revolves around relations with the US, he is gravely mistaken.

Xi is both a disciplinarian and an ideologue. He requires China’s foreign-policy establishment to pursue a global strategy based on the principles of “Xi Jinping Thought,” which shape how China assesses its national interests and responds to pressure from the US.
Chief among these principles is that preserving Xi’s leadership and Communist Party rule takes precedence over all other national interests. Close behind is enhancement of China’s global standing.
China’s defiant response to Trump’s tariff war reflects these priorities. In effect, Xi’s approach makes it nearly impossible for China to capitulate to American pressure.

What, then, does Xi’s China want? Its ultimate objective is enshrined in what Xi calls the “China Dream of National Rejuvenation,” to be fulfilled by 2050. As Olivia Cheung and I explain in our new book China’s Global Strategy under Xi Jinping, achieving this goal requires a dual pivot.
The first pivot, and the current focus of Chinese diplomacy, is to secure overwhelming support from the Global South for China’s foreign-policy agenda.

Xi has rationed his overseas travel since the Covid-19 pandemic, making his recent appearance at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek, his state visit to Egypt, and his recent visit to India particularly telling.

The second pivot is to seize Taiwan. Given Taiwan’s position within the first island chain in the Pacific Ocean and its importance to America’s strategic interests in the region, annexing it would demonstrate China’s supremacy over the US, marking the advent of Chinese global pre-eminence and the fulfillment of the China Dream. Such a mission cannot be launched until China is certain of success, and the 2050 deadline suggests Xi is in no hurry.

By courting the Global South, China seeks to forge a “common destiny for humankind” under its leadership, a Xi formulation that is regularly—and often deliberately—mistranslated by the Chinese government and media as “building a community of shared future”.
To achieve this objective, Xi promotes the “democratisation of international relations,” aimed at transforming the existing international order into a China-centric one.

In Xi’s conception, the liberal international order is of, by, and for an elitist West that represents a minority of United Nations member states and the global population. Western dominance is thus inherently undemocratic.
By contrast, the Global South—of which Xi insists China is and will remain a part of—encompasses most of the world’s countries and people.
Making the UN and other multilateral bodies accountable to the Global South would achieve the “democratisation of international relations” and enable China to shape the future international order.

More Global South countries are autocracies than democracies, which suggests that many of their leaders may find the prospect of America’s international leadership giving way to China—which regularly reassures them of their right to govern as they see fit—quite appealing.

China’s Belt and Road Initiative offers another incentive in the form of development loans without the accountability and transparency imposed by Western democracies and the multilateral development institutions they control.
The US cannot engage China effectively without recognising what drives Xi’s overtures to the Global South and his determination to transform the international order from within.
Crucially, China’s goal is not just to end American hegemony but also to discredit the idea that democracy represents the best path forward for the developing world.
It has no interest in helping the US rectify its foreign-policy mistakes. In fact, it benefits when the US is seen as a threat to global peace, security, and prosperity.

The Iran war is a case in point. While China did not want the US to attack Iran, it is benefitting significantly from the Trump administration’s use of force and its failure, despite overwhelming military superiority, to achieve any of its objectives.
The more the US alienates its traditional allies, disrupts the global economy, and harms countries in the Global South, the easier it is for China to win support.

Xi’s top priority in meeting Trump was to ensure that the summit is seen as a great success. Reaching a trade deal comes second. Helping the US extricate itself from its self-inflicted Middle Eastern mess was not even on his agenda.
If pressured, he is likely to push back hard. Nevertheless, he has every reason to engage Trump positively, deliver good optics, and benefit from America’s litany of unforced errors.
Steve Tsang is director of the SOAS China Institute at SOAS University of London.

e28d4592892d5443: Dr Hasmah Ali’s death at the age of 100 raises speculation about what role she played in the longevity of her husband, Dr Mahathir Mohamad, who is a year older and still subsisting.
Long-serving leaders of countries are known to have depended on their long-lived wives to endure by their side because of symbiotic value.
One recalls the closeness of Siti Hartinah, popularly known as Ibu Tien, to her husband, Indonesian president Suharto.

Ibu Tien died at the age of 72 in 1996. Because of the closeness of the Indonesian first couple, her death was seen as a bad omen, especially after Suharto was pressured to leave office in 1998 as a result of civil disturbances.
Unlike Ibu Tien, no controversy swirled around Hasmah during Mahathir’s long prime ministerial tenure of 22 years.
That must count as an achievement, especially in retrospect given the controversies that have come to light surrounding the tenures of other first ladies.
When Mahathir was prime minister, Hasmah knew how to be visible without being conspicuous and supportive without seeming like an appendage.
Her education — she was one of the first Malay women doctors — no doubt helped forge her equipoise.
Kwa Geok Choo, wife of another long-serving leader, Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew, was also like Hasmah in being visibly supportive without wanting or enjoying equal billing.
But it was easier for Kwa because she did not have to constantly accompany her husband in his public role as Hasmah had to in respect of Mahathir.
She was busy running a law firm that supported her family — “I am a kept man”, as Lee wryly remarked — and so she had a reason not to be constantly at her husband’s side.
Hasmah was a great help to her husband on public occasions that required an expression of grief and sympathy.

120091e268384c68: Historically, building an application on top of AWS felt less like buying well-thought-out products, and more like a trip to Home Depot. This was great in an era before we had computers that would handle the "bolting all the parts together for us" parts, but increasingly it's starting to feel a lot more dated. Today, you can use Railway, Vercel (itself a platform built atop AWS), CloudFlare, and a host of other next-generation providers who will no doubt attempt to show up self promotionally in the comments. The thing these new platforms have in common is pretty basic. They don't have the legacy baggage of having to support AWS customers accrued over the past twenty years. What they do have is a customer-forward philosophy that doesn't require customers to prove themselves worthy of using their product first. Institutional arrogance From where I sit, there's almost been a sense of institutional arrogance in AWS' view of the market, of the form "we're AWS, obviously customers will choose us." A recent testimonial on their site cites a YC founder saying "For startups of a certain scale, all roads lead to a hyperscaler like AWS." Note there's some selection bias at play: this is a quote on the AWS site itself, from a vendor whose product is explicitly aimed at making AWS easier to live with. There's clearly a baked-in sense of "we have a right to win here," which means they're in for one heck of a bad day when reality comes crashing in. AWS has shown a track record of missing breakout success stories when they're small. They like to point at Pinterest, a previous-generation darling startup that was born on AWS. Had Pinterest picked another vendor – not that there were a lot of other great options back in 2010 – an argument could be made that they'd never have found their way to Amazon, because migrations are hard and the value has to be there. You could also theorize that over the past decade-and-a-half there are times Pinterest would have jumped ship away from AWS — but again, migrations are hard. OpenAI went early with Azure, and to get Sam Altman's darling to play ball with them, AWS has had to play a catch-up game. OpenAI started running its big experiments on Azure in 2016, and Microsoft formalized the relationship with a billion dollar investment, although things seem to have gotten rockier since. Amazon, meanwhile, went from an ordinary cloud contract to "up to $50B" in investment, and OpenAI expanded its AWS commitment by $100B earlier this year. Overall, AWS seems out of the loop with the current AI zeitgeist. Take Vercel as an example. They're a platform built entirely atop AWS itself, which means that, in this new era, AWS is a wholesaler. Wholesalers don't tend to find out about the new upstart that's taking the world by storm until its growth levels off. Until that point, telling a rocket ship "hey, come for a worse experience where you get to build a lot of the things you currently take for granted, but your infrastructure bills will be smaller" is a craptastic sales pitch. The publication system for my Last Week in AWS newsletter runs mostly on Vercel rather than AWS. This costs me more per month (roughly $30 instead of "pennies") but the user experience is absolutely night-and-day different, to the point where I'm about to migrate more workloads to Vercel. User experience has always been important; increasingly the user is becoming an AI agent, and having to fight on the agent's behalf just to establish credentials to the platform, let alone do anything complicated with it, distills down to feeling like a platform hates you. Maybe it does! Maybe it just doesn't care. But there are a lot of platforms out there nowadays that do care, and that manifests in product selection. Moving up the stack, badly With the notable exception of Amazon Connect – which they are now repurposing as a brand to mean a bunch of things other than the "run your call center" service that actually succeeded – AWS's attempts to move up the stack have ended horribly. Every time they attempt to bring something to market that's a SaaS-shaped product, or is competing in a place where good user experience is going to dominate, it's just a matter of time before it ends up in the AWS graveyard. Last week, they launched what I insist on calling CloudWatch Infinidash, a new agentic experience layer for existing CloudWatch offerings. Sure enough, my agent and I took over three hours just to get the thing configured, and I wasn't exactly starting from zero. Amazon Quick (whatever that's supposed to mean, given it changes from week to week) is in much the same boat. I liked it very much at launch, but it doesn't appear to have materially changed since then, in a space where weekly change is a given. Amazon as a whole feels constitutionally incapable of being more than an (admittedly impressive) infrastructure and logistics company. The fact that they keep trying to be otherwise, yet keep failing abysmally, says that there's a self-awareness issue going on in their executive suites. Be the best wholesaler you can be The right move for AWS would be to stop trying to be a SaaS company, and emphasize being excellent as a wholesaler. Make life great for the Vercels of the world, and focus on making the experience of being a three-person company on AWS actually pleasant, not just subsidized with credits. Any "right to win" has to be earned while the customer is small, and in no way a standout. That's what builds loyalty that lasts into the hypergrowth era. Otherwise, you're just reorganizing where Home Depot put the hinges this week. ®

6c6cec276d09962f: Equipment to capture carbon dioxide from ambient air or smokestacks generally works through a sort of reversible filter. Air is passed through granules or a liquid that absorbs the CO2, then that CO2-loaded substance undergoes a process (usually heating) that causes it to let go of all that CO2. The resulting gas can be collected in a separated stream.

It’s also possible to do a similar sort of operation on a smaller scale—like inside a battery. A new study from a team led by James Buchen of the University of Delaware demonstrates an example of a battery-based electrochemical carbon-capture technique that they say is more viable than previous attempts. It has the potential to require less energy—and therefore be cheaper—than the reversible-filter designs that currently dominate.

The basic idea behind a device of this type is that hydroxide produced at the battery cathode reacts with CO2, converting it to carbonate or bicarbonate that passes through the separator membrane to the anode. There, the lower pH causes the reaction to reverse, with carbonate turning back into CO2 gas. The role of the cathode is to produce hydroxide ions; the role of the anode is to consume them.
0e75f8d0e200f5ac: The cyber criminal behind JadePuffer, the first known agentic ransomware infection reported over the summer, has also used stolen Azure identities to conduct destructive attacks on cloud storage and other resources, according to Microsoft. In July, Sysdig threat hunters uncovered JadePuffer, the first-ever documented agentic ransomware infection in which an LLM drove the entire extortion operation, from gaining initial access to compromising a production database server and destroying data. Now Redmond says that it has detected the same attacker, which it tracks as Storm-3168, up to new mischief. Over an 18-hour period in early June, Storm-3168 compromised two service principals and used these machine identities for “extensive Azure-focused resource destruction” and “cloud credential collection that could be used to facilitate future exfiltration,” researchers Yossi Weizman and Tushar Mudi wrote on Friday. The two compromised service principals belonged to the same cloud tenant. The crims used one of them to conduct reconnaissance and resource discovery, and the other to carry out destructive operations and credential collection. The Redmond researchers don’t know how Storm-3168 initially hijacked the service principals, but noted that an employee of the same organization previously exposed client IDs, client secrets, and tenant IDs in plaintext in a public GitHub issue. “Since the beginning of this year, we also observed repeated probing from Storm-3168 linked infrastructure against multiple Azure App services for different customers,” the duo wrote. The entire attack took about 18 hours, with the discovery piece lasting about 15 hours and 30 minutes. During this time, the compromised service principal collected detailed information about Azure Virtual Machines, subscriptions, resource groups, and resources, completing more than 300 successful read operations. “This breadth of activity would give the threat actor visibility across the organization’s Azure environment,” Weizman and Mudi wrote. About 90 minutes after the first machine identity began hoovering up Azure information, the second compromised service principal started its work, reading Azure VMs and resource groups across two subscriptions in just five seconds. According to Redmond, both of these service principals used Storm-3168 linked infrastructure, the same network fingerprint, and the user agent python-requests/2.34.2. About 16 hours after the initial target reads, the second service principal successfully discovered Azure App Service configuration stores - it was likely looking for exposed credentials, we’re told - and unsuccessfully attempted to find Azure OpenSearch resources. Seventy seconds after this, it also attempted a ListKey operation against a non-existent storage account. Then, the destruction began. During this part of the operation, the compromised service principal attempted more than 150 destructive or credential-stealing attempts in 35 minutes. The destructive activity only lasted about 7 minutes with the machine identity attempting to delete more than 100 Azure Storage accounts. Most of these were successful, although Azure resource locks and storage account-level deletion did block a few. Additionally, the attacker deleted an Azure Key Vault, Function App, App service plan, all of which belonged to the same resource group and likely supported the Function app. “The same service principal also attempted to delete multiple Azure SQL databases in parallel with the storage account deletions mentioned earlier, but every deletion attempt failed because it used an unsupported API version for the Azure SQL database resource type,” Weizman and Mudi wrote. About 28 minutes after the destruction ended, “the same service principal made an inventory request for Azure Storage Accounts and sent more than 30 successful ListKeys requests, asking ARM to return each storage account’s access keys,” they added. “These storage accounts included Azure Site Recovery related storage accounts.” Multiple unsuccessful deletion attempts were also made against Azure Site Recovery locks and Azure Backup protection locks protecting storage accounts. According to Microsoft, the destructive activity - deleting numerous Azure resources, while also targeting backup and recovery-related resources - seems to indicate that Storm-3168 was setting up a ransomware attack. “Taken together, the resource destruction, attempts to interfere with recovery mechanisms, and collection of credentials that could provide access to data are consistent with tactics that can support ransomware and extortion operations,” Weizman and Mudi wrote. However, no ransom note was ever sent. "We did not observe a ransom note or confirm successful data exfiltration in the activity described here," they wrote. ®
883c642fa84adfe0: The cost of healthcare in general is a debilitating, pre-existing condition for Americans. But the high prices of prescription drugs usually stand out as a pain point. While there are many insidious reasons why Americans pay more—often far more—for their medicines than people in peer countries, exploitation of the US patent system is an obvious one.

A study published Monday in JAMA highlights just how much patent exploitation has grown since 1990. In that time, researchers found that the number of patents on small-molecule drugs has more than tripled, going from an average of 2.1 patents per drug approved in 1990 to 6.9 for those approved in 2019.

Most of the growth was in "nonprimary" patents—patents that generally aren't related to a drug's active ingredient, but are instead for things like minor tweaks to a drug's nonactive ingredients, updates to the way the drug is used, or the design of specialty delivery devices, such as auto-injectors. Together, those extra patents on an individual drug can create what's called a "patent thicket," which delays the release of affordable generics on the market, keeping drug prices higher for longer without actual clinical advancements.

7a3c9b831d182222: Most LLMs are great at answering prompts, but fall short when it comes to navigating around the desktop in Windows or Linux. French AI model dev H unveiled a pair of computer use models on Monday aimed at handling graphical user interfaces (GUIs). Throughout computing history, computer use largely falls into three categories: command line interfaces (CLIs), application programming interfaces (APIs), and GUIs. AI agents can easily plug into the first two, but navigating desktop environments and applications that often prioritize form before function remains an ongoing challenge. H's Holo 4 family of models aims to address this challenge by enabling relatively small but capable models to tackle all three computer use scenarios including pointing, clicking, scrolling, and typing their way through graphical interfaces originally meant for us meatbags. Fine tuned using supervised training and reinforcement learning, Holo 4 is built atop Alibaba's Qwen 3.8 27B and Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B models. And by optimizing for CLIs, APIs, and GUIs, H claims that its models achieve far greater versatility than pure computer use models might otherwise. Alongside Holo 4, H has also updated its Holotron model, which is based on Nvidia's Nemotron 3, with similar capabilities. In one example, the company showed Holo 4 27B taking advantage of FreeCAD's macro function to programmatically design a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower rather than manually building it using primitives like cubes. In another demo, H did the opposite using extruded shapes to recreate the company's logo, showing the model's flexibility. Curiously, this doesn't mean that they're cheaper. In fact, while the company shows higher scores, in many cases the models end up costing more per task. Given what we know about Qwen 3.8 27B, this is likely due to Holo 4 using substantially more "thinking" tokens in order to arrive at a final result relative to something like GPT 6 Luna, which doesn't perform as well in the OSWorld 2.0 benchmark, but costs substantially less. Having said that, the open weights models' diminutive size means that researchers, AI enthusiasts, and enterprises should be able to run them on relatively modest hardware. A 24 GB Nvidia RTX 3090 should be more than capable of running these models at 4-bit precision. H clearly expects users to do just that since alongside BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 weights, it's also made a Llama.cpp (and by extension LM Studio and Ollama)-friendly GGUF version of the model available for download on Hugging Face. The model dev says that it also plans to release DSpark draft weights in order to speed up inference using a technique called speculative decoding. We've explored this performance-enhancing inference tech in the past, but in a nutshell it uses a small model to guess the outputs of a larger model. When it works, users experience a speedup in token processing and generation and, when it doesn't, it falls back to the base model ensuring no loss in output quality. However, the models aren't worth much without a harness. H has developed several agentic harnesses including its open source HAI-Agents harness, which is available for download on its GitHub. However, in theory the models should work with third-party computer use harnesses. H isn't the only model dev focused on computer use applications. At AWS' Re:Invent conference last year, the company announced its own set of computer-use models. Meanwhile, the big three American model labs, OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic, are also investing in this capability, perhaps because escaping their sandbox sometimes requires pushing a button. ®

4f9541e13381db10: The infamous Carrington Event of 1859 has long been considered the first extreme space weather event, but there have been reports of minor disturbances to telegraph equipment during geomagnetic storms since the late 1840s. In 2013, scholars discovered an anonymous report published in 1871 in Nature describing how a "very intense magnetic disturbance" disrupted rail travel in Exeter on the southern coast of England in October 1841. If accurate, this would be the earliest such account. However, according to a paper published in the journal Space Weather, that 1841 date is most likely a typo, with the real railway disruption occurring several years later.

"Space weather is often discussed as a modern challenge because of our dependence on technologies such as satellites, communications systems and electricity networks," said co-author Jim Wild of Lancaster University. "What this study shows is that society has been experiencing the effects of space weather on technology for almost as long as electrical technologies have existed. The Exeter train delay is a fascinating story because it sits right at the point where emerging technologies first began to encounter the realities of the space environment."

The Carrington Event remains the most powerful geomagnetic storm in the scientific record, with strong auroral displays occurring all over the world, causing sparking and even a few fires in telegraph stations. Some of the auroras were so bright that people reported being able to read the newspaper by their light. The telegraph was a relatively new technology at the time, having first emerged in the 1830s, and the geomagnetically induced current—from a likely coronal mass injection from the Sun—knocked out telegraph systems. Some operators found they were still able to transmit and receive messages even after disconnecting the power supply, relying just on the powerful auroral current.

eea3badab1c03a5d: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Last Wednesday, Anthropic announced that earlier this year it had launched a molecular biology lab, where Claude agents read and conjecture about hard biology problems and human scientists run experiments on what they report. And this AI-powered lab, the company said, had made its first discovery.

To understand what Anthropic says its system did, imagine you’re flipping through a library of millions of DNA sequences, amassed as scientists sequence more and more of the living world. One step toward a breakthrough might be finding a peculiar sequence that encodes an interesting enzyme, perhaps. Then you’d need to figure out what that enzyme does and, eventually, how to manipulate it to do something useful.

What Anthropic says its system of 950 agents found after 21 hours was not a brand-new sequence. The agents instead flagged a repeating pattern surrounding a known enzyme, a particular pattern Anthropic said hadn’t been catalogued before. But if you read through Anthropic’s announcement, which calls this pattern “reminiscent” of what led to the gene-editing technology CRISPR that “has already transformed science and medicine,” it sounds as if this army of agents really found something of note.

These claims have angered some biologists. A viral post from one, subsequently endorsed by the chair and CEO of the drugmaker Eli Lilly, said that “finding a weird cluster of genes and repeats is often the easy part. The hard part, and where the real discoveries come from, is figuring out what the system actually does.” The agents helped with some laboratory grunt work, in other words. But a discovery it is not.

It’s a reminder that even if AI does something impressive—like finding a pattern in a mass of biological data that would be difficult to perceive with human eyes alone—the result itself may not constitute a breakthrough for science. What is novel for AI may be routine, unsurprising, or simply not that consequential to a biologist.

Muddying the issue further, Mario Rodríguez Mestre, a biologist at the University of Copenhagen, said over the weekend that his team had already discovered this particular pattern, the New York Times reported. Mestre, who regularly chatted with Claude in his work, wondered whether Anthropic’s team had learned from his conversations. Anthropic denies this, but Mestre says he’s stopping all use of Claude anyway.

Part of the problem here is that AI companies aren’t presenting their systems simply as tools scientists can use, like microscopes or supercomputers. They’re insisting that the AI systems are making discoveries themselves. To some, that approach is incompatible with how science actually works, with new knowledge more typically emerging from collaboration and an ever-growing arsenal of tools.

It’s also making people more skeptical of genuine progress when it happens. Whittling 200,000 candidates down to a few worth exploring is no small feat; it is legitimate scientific work. The fact that a general-purpose chatbot could do that work is notable, even if humans helped steer it and ultimately ran the experiments. But once the standard is whether Claude itself made a discovery, all that becomes evidence for one side or the other in a debate that has only two answers: breakthrough or bust.

Once we’re judging AI by whether it has made a discovery, it’s also tempting to shift the goalposts even after it really does seem to notch a win. Earlier this month, OpenAI said its own team agents had cracked a million-dollar problem in mathematics. But a couple of weeks later, nearly every AI skeptic in my feed was sharing an article asking whether it was the math problem that really mattered.

To be clear, the piece did not argue that OpenAI’s solution was wrong. Instead, it argued that the particular result may not be the one mathematicians care most about. Throw in the accusation by a mathematician that the models may have used some of his work without credit, and people are left thinking either OpenAI cheated or the solution wasn’t important anyway. Or both.

That’s part of what concerns Lucas Harrington, the biologist who wrote the post critiquing Anthropic’s announcement. He closed with a suggestion: AI companies, he said, should “set the bar high now, so that when an AI actually discovers a fundamentally new biological mechanism, everyone appreciates how big a deal it is.” But as OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei race to one-up each other, raising the bar for scientific breakthroughs by AI might be the last thing on their minds.

331195bd439f3062: EVENT: Count the copies. The one on the NAS. The one somebody pulled over the VPN to work on at home. 84218f9201d76660: Microsoft has unveiled its shiny new Copilot super app alongside an “evolved” pricing model to go with it, which means that customers will keep paying for a subscription and then cough up more when they want the really clever stuff. The company outlined the changes alongside its expanded vision for Copilot, which is being turned into a single AI work hub spanning chat, Office apps, coding, and increasingly autonomous agents. Microsoft calls the new pricing setup a combination of a User Subscription License (USL), charged per user per month, and Usage-Based Billing (UBB), which charges according to how much work Copilot does. The regular subscription pays for what Microsoft calls “Everyday AI.” That's Copilot Chat, plus Copilot in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams. Users can pick which model they want, or leave it to Auto, which chooses based on accuracy, speed, and cost. Then there's “Advanced AI.” Customers wanting Copilot to get stuck into more compute-hungry agentic work will also need usage-based billing (UBB). Microsoft says that this includes Cowork, Code, Autopilot, new agentic experiences in SharePoint, and frontier models including Astra and Fable. Crucially, those UBB charges are on top of the user subscription, not an alternative to it. The meter itself isn't entirely new. Microsoft has already used consumption-based pricing for some AI services, including Cowork, and Copilot Credits provide the common currency for eligible services billed by usage. What's changing is how central that model will become as Microsoft pushes Copilot further into agent territory. Exactly how many credits disappear depends on what Copilot is asked to do. Microsoft says consumption can vary by the models used, how much context it has to retrieve, how long the task runs, and which tools it calls. More complicated, multi-step jobs can therefore chew through more credits than simpler tasks. Redmond isn't leaving admins completely at the mercy of an enthusiastic employee and a hungry AI agent. Usage-based features have to be enabled through a billing policy, and administrators can impose organization- and user-level spending limits, configure alerts, and monitor consumption from the Microsoft 365 admin center. That will require a mindset shift for organizations used to knowing what their Copilot seats will cost, according to Simon Baxter at analyst TechMarketView. “Customers that want these agentic capabilities will have to adopt a consumption mindset, along with the cost governance that goes with it,” Baxter said. He pointed to Microsoft's new FinOps tools for managing spending policies, credit approvals, and model access as evidence that Redmond knows customers will need help keeping tabs on the meter. Code and Autopilot could be particularly interesting for whoever holds the purse strings because they're designed to carry on working once they're set up. As Baxter put it, “an agent working without prompts is no longer tied to someone sitting at a keyboard.” That could prove awkward for public sector organizations accustomed to budgeting by headcount. Baxter pointed to NHS England's Copilot rollout, where license allocations across 505,000 staff give buyers a cost that they can plan around. Putting agents used for jobs such as complaints handling or freedom of information requests on a meter leaves trusts with a variable cost and, at least initially, little usage history on which to base a forecast. Microsoft's attempts to bundle Copilot with subscriptions and charge accordingly have already attracted some unwanted attention. The UK's Competition and Markets Authority opened an investigation in July into whether customers were properly informed when Microsoft added Copilot to consumer Microsoft 365 subscriptions and moved them onto more expensive plans unless they opted for a cheaper Classic alternative. This time, Microsoft is drawing a clearer line between the Copilot included in a subscription and the more ambitious stuff that costs extra. That’s becoming more important as Copilot itself grows from a chatbot bolted onto Microsoft's existing applications into what the company is pitching as a “super app.” The super app, then, comes with a super-app-sized ambition – and a meter for the bits that require the most horsepower. ®

7fc340f97629bdc5: The Dutch government is backing an effort to build a FOSS workplace for public administration, including a desktop operating system based on NixOS. The DAWO Project has been gestating for some months, but it just got a lot more visible thanks to an in-depth report on Dutch tech news site Tweakers.net. DAWO stands for "Digitaal Autonome Werkomgeving Overheid," or "Digital Autonomous Government Work Environment." Rather than a single product, its blueprint combines replaceable components for the operating system, cloud infrastructure, AI, communications, and collaborative working. Development remains at an early stage, but small-scale pilots are already under way within Dutch public bodies. The work acquired official status in July, when the Dutch government's ICBR – the Interdepartmental Committee on Government Operations – commissioned three government IT providers to develop a standardized, more sovereign digital workplace: DICTU, SSC-ICT and the ICT division of DUO, the Education Executive Agency. The wider blueprint comes from the Ministry of the Interior and Kingdom Relations, or BZK. Its components include MijnBureau, a self-hosted workplace suite built from projects including Nextcloud, Collabora, Element and OpenProject. The MijnBureau developers are also collaborating with France's La Suite and aligning their work with Germany's openDesk. Regular Register readers will probably recognize the name openDesk: it's featured in several recent stories. OpenDesk is the suite that the International Criminal Court is adopting following US sanctions against senior court officials. (Tweakers mentions these sanctions as being a motivating factor behind the Dutch efforts.) The ICC is based in the Netherlands, in The Hague. According to a Reuters report, the Trump administration is planning wider sanctions against the ICC. OpenDesk is also a core part of the moves in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, as we reported in July, and those in Switzerland which we covered earlier this month. Back in April, the Association of Netherlands Municipalities, or VNG, announced that four municipalities were taking part in the trials. Tweakers reports that the number has since doubled to eight – still a small fraction of the country's hundreds of municipalities. The project publishes code through the BZK's government-hosted Forgejo instance, with repositories also available through Codeberg for outside contributors. For its client OS, the project initially experimented with openSUSE, then Fedora, before settling on NixOS. The Reg FOSS desk has written about NixOS several times, including its radical approach to package management and the arrival of NixOS 22.11. NixOS offers more than a conveniently Dutch pedigree. It is not controlled by a commercial vendor, while its declarative configuration and reproducible deployments make it attractive for managing and auditing large fleets of machines. The Nix packaging system project was founded by a Dutchman, Eelco Dolstra; the first version of the NixOS distro built with it by another, Armijn Hemel; and the NixOS Foundation is based in the Netherlands. The Nix community has not been without controversy. In 2023, conference organizers withdrew sponsorship from US autonomous weapons vendor Anduril following objections from contributors. The dispute fed into a broader argument over project governance that culminated the following year in a fork called Auxolotl. FOSS projects have little control over who uses their code, while attempts to restrict particular users can create problems of their own. Government interest does, however, bring money and momentum. As we noted following the launch of Euro-Office in April and Collabora's AI-infused CODE suite in June, the scent of public sector cash is proving highly effective at stimulating activity and cooperation in the FOSS world. ®

96b4de0a983a93fe: Europe is one of the world's largest markets for AI datacenter infrastructure, but its own local companies capture only a fraction of the value, because overseas suppliers dominate chips, servers, and cloud infrastructure. According to the Global Electronics Association (GEA), EU-headquartered companies account for only six percent of the bloc's datacenter semiconductor market, seven percent of server manufacturing and assembly, and eight percent of cloud infrastructure. Its report, "From Chips to Systems: Building an End-to-End EU Strategy for Data Centre, Cloud Infrastructure and AI," says that Europe's Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) aims to at least triple the bloc's datacenter capacity within five to seven years. The association argues that Europe needs policies to develop its own industrial ecosystem and capture more of the "unprecedented demand for servers, electronic systems and semiconductor components" CADA is expected to stimulate. Europe has fallen behind other regions in much of the electronics supply chain. Taiwan dominates contract chip manufacturing and produces most of the world's leading-edge processors, many of them designed by American companies, while South Korean and US suppliers dominate the memory market. Most major server makers are American, with China's Lenovo a notable exception. US companies also dominate networking and storage, leaving Europe with few large suppliers of its own. The report recommends that the EU pursue an end-to-end strategy for the datacenter supply chain, using European demand to encourage private investment while enticing global technology and manufacturing companies to expand production within the bloc. Its case rests partly on the claim that servers, driven by AI processing requirements, have become the primary growth driver of the entire electronics industry since 2024, overtaking other segments. It points to forecasts that expect servers to become the largest electronics segment by 2030, ahead of smartphones or automotive electronics. The report also identifies datacenter, cloud, and AI infrastructure as the most strategically important market for EU technological sovereignty. Server farms constitute the critical infrastructure on which a large number of essential services now depend, and the cloud services that run on them are now integral to the design, manufacture, and operation of many physical goods. GEA argues that supporting individual parts of the supply chain in isolation will not create a competitive European industry. It points to the Chips Act 2.0 and CADA as steps in the right direction, but says that other industrial policy instruments will need to match them. "For the first time, printed circuit boards, electronic manufacturing services, advanced packaging, and substrates sit alongside semiconductor fabrication as explicit targets of European industrial strategy," it says. The report acknowledges that Europe cannot realistically build this supply chain using EU-headquartered companies alone. It says policymakers should use the "attractiveness and growth of the EU market to encourage global leaders to expand their manufacturing footprint in Europe." That could involve partnerships with European technology companies and research organizations, spreading manufacturing expertise through the region's electronics industry. The proposal echoes the Trump administration's push to rebuild American manufacturing, although it relies more on incentives than on tariffs or threats to exclude foreign products unless their manufacturers establish US production. Nevertheless, the GEA says that the European objective should be to progressively anchor a greater share of the end-to-end value chain within Europe. Whether EU members have the collective will to do this is another question, as is whether it is possible to reverse the continent's deep dependence on overseas technology. ®
